Counterpoint. The art of combining two or more independent melodic lines that sound simultaneously, each with its own rhythmic and harmonic character. The lines move in relation to each other through parallel, contrary, or oblique motion while maintaining harmonic unity, creating texture and complexity that defines much of Western classical music.

The term comes from the Latin punctus contra punctum, meaning point against point, referring to note-against-note composition. In strict counterpoint, every interval between simultaneous notes follows codified rules. Perfect consonances appear in certain positions, and parallel fifths and octaves are forbidden. Free counterpoint relaxes these rules in favor of musical expressiveness and is used in much Baroque and later music.

Bach was the master of counterpoint, particularly in his Art of Fugue and Musical Offering, which explore extreme contrapuntal techniques. Fugue, canon, and round are the primary forms built on contrapuntal principle. The technique requires each line to be singable and interesting in its own right, not merely harmonic filler. A fugue is the most sophisticated contrapuntal form, built on strict subject-and-answer imitation. Polyphony is the broader texture of multiple simultaneous melodic lines, of which counterpoint is the most disciplined subset. Sonata form often incorporates contrapuntal techniques, especially in its development sections, where different melodic ideas interweave in strict harmonic relationship.
